solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Where wine is produced, drink out of bag

indicators.note: read as 'outside of', so one piece sits on the outer side of the other and wraps it

parts.note: a beer, the crossword's favourite drink
a sac is a pouch or bag, as in biology

explanation.surface: Someone describes a vineyard where wine is drunk straight out of a bag, like boxed wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the wine region of north-east France on the German border; 'out of' here means outside, not 'drunk from'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alsace is a French region famous for its white wines, so it is a place where wine is made.

clue.text: Charges a levy for hearing

indicators.note: something meant for hearing is to be listened to, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: a levy is a tax; said quickly the two words run together

explanation.surface: A court charges someone a fee for a hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' and 'levy' both look financial, but the definition is charges in the military sense: rushes at an enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge is to rush forward in assault, so cavalry charges are assaults on an enemy line.

clue.text: Of course it will happen

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a casual interjection of agreement, certainly
second meaning: a certainty, an event bound to occur

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one breezy reassurance, but it splits into the reply 'certainly!' and the noun for a certainty.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase serves both as a relaxed yes in conversation and as a noun for a bet or outcome guaranteed to come off.

clue.text: Catholic wants to overhaul beliefs

definitions.note: plural definition for a singular noun; a credo is a whole set of beliefs

parts.note: C is a standard abbreviation for Catholic
to redo something is to rework or overhaul it

explanation.surface: A Catholic is keen to reform church doctrine.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the answer is the Latin 'I believe' that opens the Catholic Creed.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a statement or system of principles held by a person or group, a personal creed.

clue.text: A brief search around prison for continentals

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: FRISK, to search a person, with its tail cut off
'the can' is slang for jail

explanation.surface: Guards give continental visitors a quick pat-down at the jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Continentals' usually means mainland Europeans to a British reader; here it is people from another continent entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of the continent of Africa are inhabitants of a continent, hence continentals in a literal sense.

clue.text: See finished

parts.note: to see what someone means is to follow it
when you are through, you are done

explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the two words mean 'see something to its end'; read piece by piece, each word gives one half of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To follow through is to continue a task until it is complete, to see it done rather than leave it half-made.

clue.text: One simple design, or a museum piece?

indicators.note: a piece is a part cut from a larger whole, so the letters are lifted from the words before it

parts.note: runs from the middle of the first word into the start of the last

explanation.surface: A curator wonders whether a plain design counts as a museum exhibit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Simple' looks like an adjective describing the design; it is an old noun for a fool, so 'one simple' is a simpleton.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple, in old usage, is a foolish or uneducated person, which is exactly what an ignoramus is.

clue.text: Hannibal's men fed in the morning

parts.note: past tense of eat
a.m., ante meridiem

explanation.surface: Hannibal's soldiers have breakfast before marching on Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: Hannibal suggests the Carthaginian general and his army, but he is Hannibal Smith, leader of the 1980s TV team.
explanation.definitionFit: In the television series The A-Team, Colonel John 'Hannibal' Smith commands the squad of ex-soldiers.

clue.text: Bone in back that I'm unsure about

parts.note: the stern is the back of a ship
the hesitant noise made when unsure

explanation.surface: Someone has a pain in a bone of the back but cannot say which.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface places the bone in the back, but the sternum is the breastbone at the front of the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: The sternum is the flat breastbone joining the ribs at the front of the chest, a bone of the skeleton.

clue.text: Bad indeed, but nearly ignored

indicators.note: something bad has gone wrong or gone off, so these letters are in a spoiled, jumbled order

parts.note: all fifteen letters, used as written

explanation.surface: Someone admits a misdeed was bad, but argues it was more or less overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad indeed' looks like one phrase of judgement, but 'Bad' alone is the signal and 'indeed' joins the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn a blind eye is the idiom for deliberately overlooking something, pretending not to notice it.

clue.text: Sunday goes by, cryptic is ultimately unsolvable

indicators.note: cryptic means obscure or encoded, so the letters are disguised by rearrangement

parts.note: used letter for letter

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the closing letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the little word

explanation.surface: A solver complains that a week passes and the Sunday puzzle still defeats them.
explanation.walkthrough: A wry self-reference: the Sunday Times cryptic jokes about its own toughness, with 'cryptic' doing the mixing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is anybody's guess cannot be known or worked out, so it is a puzzle with no reliable solution.

clue.text: Soft bed gets an award

parts.note: a cot is a small bed, especially for a baby
a Tony is the American theatre award

explanation.surface: A comfortable bed wins a prize for its softness.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tony Awards honour Broadway theatre, much as the Oscars honour film.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cottony has the fluffy, downy texture of cotton wool, so it feels gentle and yielding to touch.

clue.text: Warning about extremely angular small strokes?

definitions.note: the question mark flags a definition by example: a stroke is one kind of rower

indicators.note: about here means around, so one piece goes round the outside of the other

parts.note: an omen is a sign of things to come

indicators.note: at the extremes means at both ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: its first and last letters
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A warning to be careful about tiny angular brushstrokes, perhaps from an art teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strokes' suggests brushwork or illness, but in rowing the stroke is the oarsman who sets the pace for the crew.
explanation.definitionFit: In a racing crew the stroke is the rower nearest the stern who sets the rhythm, so strokes are rowers.

clue.text: Tell me there's one bird in fountain

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so these letters go within the other piece

parts.note: a spout is a jet or fountain of water
the Roman numeral for one
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a bird has landed in the fountain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell me' sounds like the start of a question; it is the definition, an impatient demand to say what you mean.
explanation.definitionFit: Spit it out is the idiom urging a hesitant speaker to say whatever they are holding back, so it is a demand to be told.

clue.text: What's the sense of home schooling?

parts.note: being in means being at home
tuition is teaching or instruction

explanation.surface: A sceptic asks what the point of home schooling is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's the sense of' reads as 'what's the point of'; the definition is sense as a faculty, a sixth sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Intuition is a kind of instinctive knowing without reasoning, often called a sixth sense or gut feeling.

clue.text: PC connection lines with marks on both sides

parts.note: M for mark, the old German currency; one at the front
an ode is a poem, lines of verse
the second mark, closing the other side

explanation.surface: A computer cable labelled with marks at each end.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'marks' supplies two Ms, one either side of the poem; M is the abbreviation for the Deutschmark.
explanation.definitionFit: A modem is the device that links a computer to the internet over a phone or cable line.

clue.text: In good shape, dog gets home in spring

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it, so the second piece goes inside the first

parts.note: taken as written
at home is in
a well is a spring of water

explanation.surface: A healthy dog finds its way back home in springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In spring' looks like the season, but 'in' is the insertion signal and spring is a water source.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone doing well is thriving or healthy, which is what being in good shape means.

clue.text: Time following near darkness

indicators.note: following means coming after, so this piece is placed at the end

parts.note: nigh is an old word for near
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: As time passes, darkness falls.
explanation.walkthrough: The order flips: 'Time following near' puts the T after the word for near.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is the period of darkness between sunset and sunrise, so the two words are close synonyms.

clue.text: Something thrown up in the air, caught by little girl

indicators.note: something caught is held fast, so these letters are gripped inside the other piece

parts.note: a pet form of Helen or Eleanor
to be announced, still undecided

explanation.surface: A ball is tossed into the air and a small girl catches it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface splits after 'thrown up in the air', but the definition stops at 'thrown'; 'up in the air' means undecided, as plans are.
explanation.definitionFit: A netball is the ball used in the team game of netball, so it is an object that gets passed and thrown.

clue.text: Moorland area hike — sorry, rambling

indicators.note: rambling means wandering about aimlessly, so the letters stray from their order

parts.note: used letter for letter

explanation.surface: A walker apologises mid-hike on the moors, having wandered off course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rambling' fits the walking scene perfectly; it is also the signal. Yorkshire is a large county in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Yorkshire contains the North York Moors and much of the Pennine moorland, making it a region known for its moors.

clue.text: Be humiliated, and the rest will stop a fight

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so the plug surrounds the small piece it fills

parts.note: etc., et cetera, 'and the rest'
taken as written
a row is a noisy quarrel

explanation.surface: A loser is humbled while the others step in to break up a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop a fight' suggests intervening; the abbreviation instead closes round the letter A.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat crow is the idiom for being forced to admit you were wrong, swallowing your pride in humiliation.

clue.text: Flying out with band on the road

indicators.note: flying letters are scattered through the air and land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a ring is a band, as round a finger

explanation.surface: A rock group flies out to play gigs on tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' wants to be the musicians in this scene; it is a circle of metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A band or performer that is touring travels from venue to venue, which is what being on the road means in music.

clue.text: Inappropriate force will break one

indicators.note: to break into something is to burst its way inside, so one piece enters the other

parts.note: a unit is a single thing, one
F is the physics symbol for force

explanation.surface: Using too much force will snap the part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inappropriate force' reads as one phrase, but the definition ends after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unfit for a purpose is unsuitable or not appropriate to it, so the two are near synonyms.

clue.text: Good standing?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: erect, vertical, on one's feet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Good standing' looks like the set phrase for a sound reputation; split, each word is a separate sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means both honourable in character and physically vertical, as a post or person on their feet.

clue.text: Right-on party piece

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
taken as written
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A politically correct party trick or song for a gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right-on' reads as one hyphenated adjective, meaning fashionably progressive; the hyphen hides a break between two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical composition with a recurring theme, often a final movement, so it is a piece of music.

clue.text: Armed conflict that takes two seconds

definitions.text: Armed conflict that takes two seconds

parts.words: Armed conflict that takes two seconds
parts.note: surface reading: a war so brief it is over in a couple of moments
setter's reading: seconds are the assistants who attend each fighter in a formal duel, one per side

explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' looks like units of time, but in duelling each combatant has a second, so a duel needs two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase names a duel fought to settle a point of honour, a formal fight with weapons and attendants.

clue.text: Classics expert one can put in register

indicators.note: to put something in is to insert it, so this piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a register is a list of names
a tin is a can
a, the indefinite article, means one

explanation.surface: A clerk asks which classics scholar can be entered on the register.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One can' reads as 'someone is able', but it is two nouns: a single tin.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latinist is a scholar of the Latin language and literature, a central branch of classical studies.

clue.text: Huge parts shine, which is not actually striking

definitions.note: the definition is a description; the answer is a noun for such a protest

indicators.note: to part something is to split it open, so the other piece is separated around this one

parts.note: to glow is to shine softly
OS is short for outsize, the clothing size

explanation.surface: A sparkling but unimpressive sight: big pieces gleam, yet the effect is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' means impressive in the surface; in the definition it means on strike. A go-slow is a British form of industrial protest.
explanation.definitionFit: In a go-slow, workers deliberately work slowly as protest instead of walking out, so they are not on strike.
